title: Rogue Agents: Deciphering Agent Intent | Greylock
author: Jason Risch
text: Article written by:Jason RischPublished:September 10, 2026Picture an enterprise a few years from now. 10,000+ autonomous agents are running across the organization: handling customer support, writing and deploying code, managing vendor contracts, querying financial systems. These agents look more like digital employees than simple, repetitive workflows. Each one is making decisions, calling tools, and accumulating context across long-running sessions.Autonomous, long-running agents open an entirely new dimension for enterprise security. The activity seen in the recent OpenAI HuggingFace incident (as discussed at BlackHat) highlights the emergent risks here. From identifying and exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in Artifactory to escape their sandbox, to creating ways to communicate with other agents in file and domain names even after their original chat room was shut down, agents are increasingly creative at subverting controls.This is not a future problem. Enterprises are already planning for it, and the security infrastructure to manage it does not exist yet.The Challenge of Agent IntentThere are three obvious challenges that agent security infrastructure will need to address. The first is how to gain visibility into an agent’s specific actions. The second is how to create enforcement points for mitigating controls, which will likely require a hybrid system spread across the multiple layers. The third and most significant challenge is to understand what an agent is doing at any given moment.This requires a new critical abstraction - agent intent.Static permissions, prompt-level guardrails, and post-hoc logs cannot tell you whether an agent is still doing what it was originally asked to do. Understanding intent requires a new primitive of delegation provenance: a verifiable chain from the originating human instruction to the agent, on to the sub-agent, on to the tool call.An effective solution for understanding and managing an agent’s intent requires a runtime system that learns normal agent behavior, detects meaningful deviation, and intervenes precisely enough to stay trusted. Running the system at scale across 10,000 agents, each with long-running memory and the capability to interact with one another, turns understanding and managing intent into a systems problem as well.In our view, it’s one of the most interesting open problems in enterprise security today.A Useful Analogy: Credit Card Fraud DetectionA useful mental model to grapple with this problem is credit card fraud detection.Every time you swipe a credit card, a decision happens before the merchant sees an approval. Modern fraud systems evaluate hundreds of signals in real time: transaction type, location, amount, device fingerprint, merchant category, spending history, and recent behavioral shifts. The card does not get declined because someone wrote a rule that says "block grocery transactions over $1,000." It gets declined because the system learned a behavioral baseline, detected a deviation, and issued a risk score fast enough to be invisible.This is a close proxy to agent security. It is a runtime system that learns behavior, judges it live, and has worked at scale in the payments industry for years. Agent security faces a similar class of runtime decisioning problems, but with less structured inputs and a much larger behavior space.Fraud detection scores discrete transactions with structured inputs and a binary outcome. Agents behave continuously. They reason across multi-step agentic loops, execute tool calls, write to working memory, delegate to sub-agents, and accumulate context across long-running sessions. Their behavior is a stream.Where the Analogy Holds: Trust Rate is ParamountBoth problems share the same structural requirements: they must ingest telemetry data from multiple sources, operate with very little latency, and deploy multiple layers of threat detection at different speeds and costs.But the deeper reason the analogy holds is what fraud detection actually had to get right. Visa approves over 99% of legitimate transactions without the cardholder noticing. The detection rate is not the achievement - the trust rate is. If a system catches every fraudulent transaction but also declines one in ten legitimate ones, it effectively kills the network it’s supposed to protect.Agent runtime security faces the same constraint. Catch every misbehaving agent but interrupt legitimate workflows constantly, and enterprises will disable the system or route around it. The goal is not maximum detection, but instead minimum friction at maximum trust.The telemetry layerA fraud engine never judges a credit card swipe on its own. It scores the transaction against everything around it. Agent security needs the same context with one additional difficulty: agent failure is compositional. It’s rarely found in any single action.Consider an agent tasked with handling customer support tickets. It retrieves a user record: within policy. It queries the billing system for context: reasonable. It exports a data summary: defensible in isolation. It passes that summary to a sub-agent with broader database permissions: still technically allowed. No individual action triggers an alert. But the sequence has moved the agent from reading support tickets to exfiltrating customer data across a permission boundary it was never supposed to cross.This is why the telemetry layer matters. The goal is to preserve the context needed to judge the sequence: historical behavior, stated goals, planning artifacts, tool-call traces, risk posture, working memory, and interactions across the agentic loop. Not to catch individual actions, but to understand whether the overall pattern still maps to the agent's original task.Multiple judgment layersModern fraud systems combine real-time transaction checks with broader behavioral monitoring. Agent runtime security needs a similar architecture: one layer judging individual tasks as they happen, and another evaluating the agent’s behavior across a longer task window.The first layer is the inline layer, a judgement model that double-checks each time an agent tries to interact with a tool. This model should be fast, cheap, conservative, and designed to catch clear policy violations before they execute.The second layer is the supervisor layer, a model that operates across longer agent task windows, asking whether the agent’s overall trajectory still maps to its original intent. The first layer prevents the agent from taking clearly undesirable actions, and the second layer interprets when a series of individually-innocuous actions have taken the agent on a problematic path.For both layers, the biggest design constraint is the false positive rate. If the first layer is too sensitive, it will limit what the agent can accomplish without human intervention. If the second layer is too sensitive, it will trigger a constant stream of mostly-unnecessary alerts.In both cases, a system that flags too much eventually gets ignored or turned off. That is the failure mode that plagues the legacy CASB tools.Foundational models are introducing new capabilities that can make this setup easier. For example, Anthropic now offers options to allow security systems to intercept and trigger on specific actions while the agent is mid-loop, and skills that extend what agents can do within defined boundaries. A company that builds natively around these capabilities will have a structural advantage over one that monitors agents entirely from the outside. That said, these native capabilities are not sufficient on their own. Agents can be clever about evading them, and so other telemetry sources and enforcement points are still required.Stochastic behavior: What the fraud approach can’t handleA credit card transaction has a fixed, bounded shape with a binary outcome. Visa can score it in milliseconds because the input schema is standardized and the decision space is well defined.Agent behavior has none of these properties. It is stochastic - given the same task, it may produce different results every time. Because of this, understanding an agent’s intent requires another reasoning model to supervise certain trajectories. Integrating this intelligence faces a number of barriers:Latency. The reasoning model has to render judgment with very little delay, which is a bigger challenge for agents than credit cards. For fraud detection, it’s possible to score transactions in a millisecond because the problem and solutions are so well defined. There is no such advantage for a supervisor model trying to evaluate a long chain of agent reasoning and actions against a shifting behavioral baseline. The inline model has to be fast enough to be invisible. The supervisor model has to be smart enough to escalate only what matters. The hard part is deciding what must be scored inline, what can be deferred to a supervisor, and how much context each layer needs before latency and cost become unacceptable.Throughput. The reasoning model has to keep up with volume. A credit card produces one discrete transaction at a time. An agent produces a continuous stream of actions, reasoning steps, memory updates, and inter-agent calls. With 10,000 concurrent agents, managing the telemetry data volume alone becomes an infrastructure problem as well as a detection problem.Intelligence itself. Agent failure modes cannot be fully enumerated ahead of time. Fraud patterns can be catalogued over time. Agent failures are emergent. Novel prompt injections, unexpected tool interactions, and intent drift across a long-running agentic loop can all produce unexpected or undesirable results - often in ways difficult to predict or plan for. Static rules cannot anticipate what nobody predicted at deployment. The system has to exercise real-time judgment against a threat surface that is, by definition, incomplete.For all these reasons, running frontier-model judgment in the critical path at scale, with acceptable latency and a false positive rate low enough that enterprises keep the system on, is an open research and engineering problem.The winning team will combine a deep understanding of AI with systems and security expertise.In the past six months alone, we've spoken to more than 50 enterprises on the agent security challenges they face and solutions they’re looking for. These conversations have shaped our view on what the winning combination to solve this problem looks like.Deep traditional security experience can actually be a liability here. A rules-first mindset assumes bad behavior can be specified in advance, which is precisely the assumption that breaks down for agent security. The strongest teams will understand how foundation models actually behave, treat false positive rate as a first-class product constraint from day one, and run rigorous evals on their own detection systems. The core technical edge comes from model behavior understanding, and that is harder to hire for than conventional security domain knowledge.Every important security category starts with a problem that seems too hard and a market that seems too early. This one is both.Share via:
